conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had terrible diarrhea for two days—like, nonstop. Then I started vomiting and got this awful belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was there any fever or blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt feverish, but no blood. The pain started crampy, then got sharp across my upper belly—same as my usual pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis and gastroparesis, this could be a flare-up from a stomach bug. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been managing okay at home, but this time it just overwhelmed me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were given IV fluids and Dilaudid in the ER. We’ll keep you on low-dose pain meds and monitor your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars have been low. I got D50 twice already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your insulin has been reduced for now since you’re not eating much. We’ll adjust it as you start tolerating feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m worried about my G-tube feeds though—sometimes they make me feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start them slowly. Right now, your belly is tender near the G-tube site, so we’ll wait until nausea improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is a bit high, which suggests infection, but your liver and pancreas enzymes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably just a virus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. No signs of bacterial infection so far. We’re holding off antibiotics unless something changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve had bad reactions to penicillin and Bactrim before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted your allergies. No antibiotics planned unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea is better today. We’d like to restart your tube feeds at a low rate and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but go slow. I don’t want to start vomiting again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start at 20 cc/hr and increase only if you’re comfortable. A nurse will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feeds are running at 20 cc/hr. You’re doing well so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. Not nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re up to 40 cc/hr and keeping it down. We’re going to increase to 50 later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My belly pain is also less intense now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been giving low-dose IV Dilaudid, but you’re needing it less. We’ll switch to oral pain meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take tramadol at home. Can I go back on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We offered it yesterday, but you declined. If you’re comfortable, we can restart it, but your team recommends tapering off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t want it then—I felt groggy. But I’ll take it if the pain comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter. That supports a viral cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it wasn’t food poisoning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. No bacterial pathogens were found. Your body is clearing it on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried I did something wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Viruses happen. Your chronic conditions just make recovery slower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV pain meds since yesterday. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Just mild discomfort now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your blood sugars are stabilizing. We’re increasing your insulin back toward your home doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t want my diabetes to get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re following your usual regimen. You’re on glargine at night and U-500 regular insulin with feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry checked in. They say your mood and anxiety are stable on Seroquel, Valium, and trazodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sleeping better. Still anxious, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommend continuing your meds. There’s a referral out for long-term support, but no response yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like more help, but it’s hard to find someone who takes my insurance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to connect you with a provider. In the meantime, your current plan is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been at 50 cc/hr for tube feeds for two days with no issues. That’s your goal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and you’re stable on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to leave if I’m not ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t discharge you unless you’re safe. You’ll go home with hydromorphone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not tramadol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You refused it multiple times here, so we’re discontinuing it. Your primary doctor will help you taper if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’d rather not take it if I don’t have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll go home tomorrow. We’ll send you with instructions for insulin, feeds, and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my asthma? I’ve been using my inhaler more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your Advair and added ipratropium four times a day to help with any bronchospasm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s helped. I’ll keep using it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, you’ll take pantoprazole daily for stomach protection, and keep using lactulose and MiraLAX as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lidocaine patch for my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one patch daily. It’s safe to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My PCP is on vacation. Should I wait to follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dr. Patel and Dr. Kim know about your stay. Call your PCP when they’re back, or sooner if you have issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Nurse will review all instructions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: resume your insulin as before, keep feeds at 50 cc/hr, and call if pain or vomiting returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no tramadol unless my doctor says so?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Use hydromorphone only if pain is severe. And follow up with your PCP in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re discharging you to home with a clear mind and steady condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having a lot of diarrhea—up to eight times today—and I can’t keep anything down, not even my tube feeds. My blood sugar was really high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, started yesterday. I also feel this weird 'electricity' all over my body for the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll check your electrolytes. Did you eat anything different recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had seafood in ___ a few days ago. I think that might have triggered this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll test your stool to rule out infections. Your blood sugar was 497 in the ER, so we’ve already given you insulin and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My abdominal pain is about the same as usual, not worse. But I just can’t tolerate food or feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and give IV fluids. We’ll start tube feeds slowly once your nausea improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my 'electric' feeling—is that from high sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could be neuropathy from your diabetes. We’ll monitor it and adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a bacterial one. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis and gastroparesis, this may be a flare-up related to your pancreas condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I ate seafood—could that still be a factor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have irritated your system, but it doesn’t look like a foodborne infection. We’ll focus on managing your underlying conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feeds at 5 cc/hr. We’ll increase slowly if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous—I usually get pain when I start feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If you have pain, we’ll pause and reassess. You’ll have IV pain meds available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some setbacks with the feeds due to pain, so we had a team meeting to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did you decide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think your GJ tube might be clogged or not placed optimally. We’re scheduling a tube revision with interventional radiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a procedure where they replace the tube using imaging guidance. It’s not open surgery, and you’ll be awake but sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it if it might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube revision was successful. The new tube is in the right place in your jejunum. We’ll wait a few hours and restart feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hope this one works better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating the new tube well. Feeds are at 20 cc/hr with no pain so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually feel a bit better. My 'electric' feeling is less intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood sugar is also more stable—around 200. We’ve increased your long-acting insulin to 34 units nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I was on 90 units at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since you weren’t eating, we lowered it to 30 units. Now that you’re feeding again, we’re increasing it gradually to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall yesterday on your way to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I slipped. My wrist hurts, and my shoulder feels weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-rays show no fractures in your wrist or shoulder. Ortho thinks it’s a wrist sprain and possible rotator cuff issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no break?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’ve put your wrist in a splint and recommend a sling. Your PCP will order an MRI later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your magnesium is low, which might contribute to the 'electric' sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving you supplements. It should help with the nerve symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed mixed flora—likely contamination. No infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some vaginal discharge for months. Should I get checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you declined the exam. Please follow up with your PCP after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge soon. Your nutrition is stable—you’ve actually gained weight despite not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize that. I feel like I haven’t eaten in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But your albumin is normal, so you’re getting enough through the tube. We’re weaning your IV pain meds and switching to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay with that. I don’t want to stay on IV meds forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added some new meds for constipation—senna, docusate, and bisacodyl. Your narcotics cause this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some bright red blood—was that from hemorrhoids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no concern now. Keep up the bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sleep? I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding trazodone and adjusting Ambien. Also reducing zolpidem dose to avoid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge plan for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue tube feeds as tolerated. Take your new insulin dose—34 units at night. Use Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them—lactulose, senna, docusate, bisacodyl. They’ll help prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my PCP for the MRI and vaginal check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if your blood sugar goes too high or low, or if you can’t tolerate feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, walking independently, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up with your follow-ups and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in the clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my asthma. I’ve been using my inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue Advair and albuterol as prescribed. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I almost forgot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over them with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let us know if you have any questions after you get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with your PCP to coordinate care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to make sure you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. My stomach pain got way worse over the weekend. It’s in my upper belly and now it’s going to my right side. I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you said you vomited? What did it look like?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, three times last night. First like food, then yellow. No blood. I’ve also had diarrhea—five times today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chills, but no fever. I took juice this morning and it made the pain so bad I had to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started IV fluids and gave you some Dilaudid in the ER. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but still really bad. I take 6 mg Dilaudid every 4 hours at home, but it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you 0.25 mg IV Dilaudid every 3 hours as needed. That’s the same dose you had last time and we’ll stick with it for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s not enough. I need more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you’re in pain, but we need to balance relief with safety. We’ll keep monitoring and adjusting as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I also haven’t had a real bowel movement in days. I’ve tried everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a high white count and mild dehydration. We did an X-ray with contrast through your GJ tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is the tube okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is in the right place—no blockage or leak. The ultrasound also showed no abscess around the site, just some redness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on antibiotics since the ER. Do I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started vancomycin because of the redness, but since there’s no infection sign, we’ll stop after three days. Your primary doctor will check the site next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’m really worried about the constipation. I can’t keep going like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding oral naloxone to help with opioid-related constipation. It can help you pass stool without affecting pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I heard you had a bowel movement last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes! A big one. I feel so much better. Still some pain, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep you on the new bowel regimen—Colace, senna, and lactulose—to prevent this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start drinking again? I’m so thirsty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated clear liquids overnight. We’ll keep advancing your diet slowly—start with broth and jello today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugar was low this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your NPH insulin and using Humalog as needed. We’ll make sure your levels stay stable before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you’re getting tube feeds now. How are you feeling with them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay so far. No nausea. But I took some extra pills from my bag earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. For safety, we need to store your pills during your stay. They’ll be returned when you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No! That’s not fair! I need them!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re upset, but we have to follow safety rules. Security will help keep things calm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m leaving then!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Code Purple has been called. You’ll get some Ativan and Zyprexa to help you calm down. This is for your safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Sorry about earlier. I was just scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay. We’re here to help. We had a talk with your primary doctor. Your pain plan won’t be increased, even at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like it, but I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’re off IV meds, eating clears, and had a good bowel movement. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with scripts for the new bowel regimen. Keep using your regular insulin, GJ tube meds, and pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No antibiotics needed. Keep it clean. See your doctor in a week to check it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your current pain meds as directed. If it’s unmanageable, come back. But no increases without discussing with your provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your pills returned and get the discharge papers ready. You should be home by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you go. Any chest pain lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just the usual—comes and goes, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And it’s reproducible when I press here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It’s probably just muscle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely so. But mention it at your next visit. Otherwise, you’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Follow up with your team and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon, hopefully not in the hospital!

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fingers crossed!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge instructions and meds. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye!
