conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve had this squeezing pain in my belly again—right in the middle and upper part. It woke me up at night. I’ve also been throwing up and having diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the pain different from your usual abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels similar to past times, but it’s been really bad. I’ve had a fever, night sweats, and I haven’t been able to eat much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your blood sugar was high when you arrived—397—and there were ketones in your urine. That means your diabetes is under stress right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I’ve been thirsty and peeing a lot too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are classic signs of high blood sugar. We’ve already given you some insulin to help bring it down. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What about the pain? It’s really hard to deal with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it with IV fluids and IV Dilaudid for pain. We’re also giving you Compazine for nausea. You’re not eating right now, so we’re holding your tube feeds temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being NPO. When can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids once your nausea and pain improve. It might take a day or two. We want to make sure your stomach can handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had this before—sometimes it’s my gastroparesis acting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your history of gastroparesis and chronic pancreatitis makes this tricky. But your lipase level was normal, so it’s probably not a pancreatitis flare this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the diarrhea and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be viral—especially since you had cold symptoms last week. Or it could be related to your diabetes and gut motility. We didn’t get a stool sample, so we can’t confirm infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did have a cough with dark mucus. But I thought it was just a cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits. Sometimes a viral illness can trigger gut symptoms like this, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on it. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and adjust your insulin based on your intake. We’ll reassess your pain and nausea every few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The nausea isn’t as bad, but I still have some belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs are stable. The urine culture came back with mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination—nothing to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. The results suggest skin or genital bacteria got into the sample. No sign of a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. Can I try some food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll advance to a soft diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And can I take my regular meds by mouth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting your oral meds—metoclopramide, omeprazole, and your pancreatic enzymes. We’ll keep the IV pain meds for now but transition to oral soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been asking for Valium for anxiety. Can I get that more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re limiting IV Valium to avoid over-sedation. You can have your regular oral dose—10mg every 6 hours as needed. Let’s try that first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and soft foods. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I only needed one dose of Dilaudid last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds only—2mg Dilaudid tablet every 4 hours as needed. You’re also back on your full diabetic diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my insulin? Is it the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Lantus dose is staying at 50 units at bedtime. We’re continuing your sliding scale for mealtime insulin based on your blood sugar checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been checking it at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep doing that. We want to make sure your sugars stay in a safer range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days without vomiting or diarrhea. Your pain is well-controlled with oral meds. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s awesome. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular medications. We’re adjusting a few—your Remeron dose is now 15mg at night instead of 30mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still effective for sleep and appetite, but the lower dose reduces drowsiness and weight gain risks. Your Trazodone is also now 100mg instead of 200mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can handle that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow morning. You’ve been off IV meds for over 24 hours, eating regular food, and your blood sugar is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Should I be worried if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your oral Dilaudid as prescribed. If you have vomiting, diarrhea, or can’t keep food down for more than 24 hours, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep checking your blood sugar four times a day. If it’s over 300 twice in a row, or you have ketones, call your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’re alert, walking, and your vitals are stable. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I restart my tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as tolerated. If you’re eating well, you may not need them. But keep them available if your appetite drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment with Dr. ___ in a few days. They’ll review your meds and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re doing well—pain controlled, no nausea, eating normally. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been really sick—nauseous, throwing up, and my blood sugar’s been super high. Over 400. I couldn’t get insulin needles at home, so I couldn’t give myself my usual shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you notice any other symptoms with the high blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had a headache and blurry vision, but that’s better now. My stomach pain is worse though—especially in the upper middle and right side. It goes into my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain gets worse when you eat or move?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially after trying to eat. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs when you came in. Your blood sugar was 458, and your lipase was elevated, which suggests your pancreas is irritated. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis, this could be a flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So is it bad? Is it different from my usual pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like an acute episode on top of your chronic condition. But you’re not running a fever, and your lungs and heart are clear on the chest X-ray. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What are we going to do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get fluids through your IV, and we’ll control your blood sugar with insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with clear liquids once your nausea improves and your pain starts to go down. It might take a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I don’t want my sugars to stay high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you IV insulin in the ER, and your sugar dropped to 290. Now you’re back on your usual Lantus at night and Humalog as needed. We’re monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I hate when it stays high for too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain and nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, and the pain is about a 6. I haven’t thrown up since I got here, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you Dilaudid for pain and Compazine for nausea through the IV. Your white count is a bit high, but no signs of infection, so we’re not using antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is the high white count from the pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, inflammation can raise it. It’s already starting to come down, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look better. Lipase is down, and your blood sugar is 180. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea’s better. Pain’s around a 4 now. Can I try some water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you keep that down, we can advance to a soft diet later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And can I take my pills again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your omeprazole for your stomach, and your psychiatric meds—mirtazapine, trazodone, zolpidem—are still scheduled as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some broth and juice, no vomiting. Can I try something more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll try a light diabetic diet—small portions, low fat. That’s easier on your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is down to 2, and you’ve kept your meals down. We’re going to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Will my meds change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No major changes. We’re sending you home with insulin syringes—100, with three refills. Your Lantus and Humalog doses stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pain meds? I usually need more than the prescribed Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sending strong painkillers home because of your history. But your regular meds and omeprazole should help. If pain flares, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge labs look good. White count normalized, lipase is down to 64, and kidney function is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pancreatitis is getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was a mild acute episode. We’ll follow up with your PCP to make sure it fully resolves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Keep your appointment with Dr. ___ this week. Continue your diabetic diet, take your meds, and avoid alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure I don’t run out of supplies again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad we could help. Take care, and call if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having this sharp pain on my right side, especially when I walk. It comes with palpitations. And my usual stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting are still here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest pain is on the right side, sharp, worse with walking. I’ve been feeling my heart racing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how about your diabetes? Are you managing your insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t taken my short-acting insulin since Wednesday. I lost my glucometer, so I can’t check my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain why your blood sugar was high when you arrived—499. We’ll help you manage that here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My PCP started me on levofloxacin for my GJ tube site—thought it might be infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll continue that for now. We’re going to run some tests to check your chest pain and make sure your pancreas isn’t flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many admissions for this. I just want the pain under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on that. You’re getting Dilaudid for pain and insulin to bring your sugar down. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your EKG and first troponin were normal. We’ll repeat those to rule out a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of a heart attack. Your tachycardia is likely from pain or anxiety. You’re wearing a Holter monitor—cardiology will review that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my GJ tube? It’s been leaking a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. If it comes out, we may need to replace it. For now, it looks okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have a problem. You pulled your GJ tube out overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t mean to. It was uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a Foley catheter temporarily. Interventional Radiology will replace the GJ tube tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated. It’s a quick procedure under X-ray guidance. You’ll be fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The GJ tube was successfully replaced this morning. You can start taking oral meds again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed a low-grade fever and some tenderness near the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan. No free air or abscess. But there’s redness, so we’re starting clindamycin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my penicillin allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, clindamycin is safe. It’s not related to penicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever is gone, and the white count is improving. The antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My pain is better too. Can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re advancing you to a regular diet. You’re not using the tube for feeds, so oral intake is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CT shows the GJ tube is in place, no complications. Pancreas looks stable—no acute flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still chronic pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with calcifications, but no acute signs. Your pain is managed with Dilaudid, and we’re limiting extra doses to one per day to stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re letting you choose when to take that extra dose—like before procedures or when pain spikes. That way, you have some say.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar is still high—around 265. We’re worried about adjusting insulin because your eating is unpredictable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to eat more regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted endocrinology. You’ll go home on 60 units of Lantus at bedtime and a new sliding scale for Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to get a new glucometer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please do. Checking your sugars is essential to avoid highs and lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped a bit—from 14.3 to 11.9. We’re watching it. Could be from chronic disease or mild malnutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not acutely. It’s mild. Eating well and managing your gastroparesis will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Pain is controlled, eating regularly, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a couple of days. You’ll finish the 3-day clindamycin course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good. Hemoglobin is up to 12.9, white count normal, sodium improved from 132 to 136.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the rash on my arms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely not serious—maybe a reaction to a med or stress. It’s not spreading. Keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is tomorrow. You’ll go home with Dilaudid for pain, but only one pill every three hours after the first five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to see my pain doctor for refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your PCP for that. Also, continue omeprazole, your inhalers, and the new insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clindamycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it twice a day for three days. Stop after that. No refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, walking, and your pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. It was rough, but I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the clindamycin, use your new insulin doses, and follow up with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no driving when I take Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay safe. Call if you have fever, severe pain, or high blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep in touch. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re doing well. Go home, rest, and follow the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you understand to take clindamycin for three days, then stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, two capsules every six hours for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And insulin—60 units Lantus at bedtime, Humalog with meals using the new scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll get a new glucometer today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And call if your GJ site gets red or painful again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine was red earlier. Any more of that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since that one time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll note it. Could be from meds or dehydration. Stay hydrated and mention it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, you’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. You came in with worsening abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the pain started about four days ago. It’s in my upper belly, kind of wrapping around to the right side. It’s like my usual pain, but worse. I was in the hospital a few days ago but left AMA because I felt a little better. Now it’s back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you been able to keep anything down? Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been throwing up a lot. I can’t eat much. My GJ tube hasn’t been working right either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll check on that. We gave you some Zofran and Dilaudid in the ER for nausea and pain. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but still pretty bad. I need something stronger sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing it with IV Dilaudid as needed. We also did a chest X-ray to check for other issues, but your lungs look clear. The Port-A-Cath and your GJ tube are visible, but we’ll need to confirm if the tube is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t want the X-ray, but okay. Is my tube really the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be. You mentioned it wasn’t working well. We’ll look into it. For now, we’re treating this as acute on chronic pancreatitis, which fits your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I always get. But why does it keep happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chronic pancreatitis means your pancreas is already damaged. Things like poor nutrition, diabetes, and even the tube issues can flare it up. We’ll focus on controlling pain, stopping vomiting, and making sure your tube works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your blood sugar was high at 342, but your white count is normal. No signs of infection. Your electrolytes were a bit off, but we’re correcting them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sugars are always high. I take Lantus at night, but I haven’t been eating, so I wasn’t sure how much to take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your Lantus to 20 units at bedtime because you’re not eating much. When you start eating again, you’ll need to increase it. We’ll talk more about that later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I don’t like changing my insulin. I have a routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re doing this to keep your sugars safe. Too much insulin when you’re not eating can cause lows. We’ll help you adjust when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. What about my tube? Can we fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace it. The team from Interventional Radiology will do it tomorrow. You mentioned the last tube type didn’t work well for you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the MIC one. I need the other kind—the one I had before. It works better with my feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll make sure they use the one you prefer. The procedure is quick—done over a wire so they don’t have to start from scratch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is looking better. You’ve had Dilaudid and Compazine, and you haven’t vomited since yesterday. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, yeah. Still sore, but not as intense. Can I try eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can start with small sips. But we’re waiting until after your tube replacement tomorrow. We want to make sure the new tube is working before you rely on it or eat too much by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But what if the new tube doesn’t work either?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology report shows the old tube was in the right place, so the issue might be with how it’s used. The new one should work. We’ll test it after placement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your tube was successfully replaced this morning. They used the type you wanted, and it’s now in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I start my feeds now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we started a slow feed today. But we’ll monitor for residuals—if too much stays in, we may need to hold it for a bit. Your gastroparesis can slow stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate when that happens. It feels like I’m full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. We also switched your Protonix to Prevacid Solutab. It dissolves better and works in the tube. Protonix doesn’t dissolve well when crushed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as I can take it through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started concentrated tube feeds today. How are you tolerating them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. No vomiting. But I’m still not hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The feeds will help with nutrition. Your blood sugar was 251 yesterday—still high, but better. Keep taking your insulin as we adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying. But I don’t want to go low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you adjust as you eat more. For now, 20 units is safe. You’ll need to increase it later—talk to your PCP about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Pain is controlled, no nausea, and you’re tolerating the tube feeds. We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good. But what about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a one-week supply of Dilaudid—same dose you take at home. No refills, as per policy. You’ll need to see your PCP for more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also want to check the tube placement before you leave, just to be sure it’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to do that. I feel fine. The tube is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it’s important. If it’s not in the right place, your feeds could go into your stomach and cause issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just don’t want another test. Can’t we just assume it’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t assume. But if you refuse, we’ll document that. Just please check at home and call your doctor if there’s any problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re ready to discharge you. You’re alert, walking, and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your new Prevacid instead of Protonix. Take your insulin—20 units at night for now, but increase as you eat more. Call your PCP for refills and to review all your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re unsure if it’s working because you declined the check. Please verify at home. If you have pain, swelling, or can’t run feeds, call your doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check it. I think it’s fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, follow up with your PCP soon. And if pain worsens or you can’t keep fluids down, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing your records. You were transferred here for abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this pain in my upper belly for a day now. It’s the same as before—radiates to the right side. I also felt nauseous, threw up, and had diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned shortness of breath and chest pain earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, but that got better with the breathing treatments in the ER. The belly pain didn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs from the outside hospital look normal—lipase, liver tests, everything. No signs of infection or pancreatitis flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain is real. I couldn’t keep anything down. They only gave me Zofran, and it didn’t help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. We’ll manage your pain and nausea. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—to let your stomach rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no food at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll start with IV fluids and give you Dilaudid under the skin for pain. Once you’re stable, we’ll try small sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have IV Dilaudid? It works better for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using subcutaneous Dilaudid for now, which is effective. We’ll reassess your pain regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there. Not better. I feel weak and my blood sugar’s been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 223 this morning. Since you’re not eating, we’ve reduced your Lantus insulin to avoid lows. We’ll adjust when you start eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I really need something stronger for pain. Can I get the IV version?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your exam shows mild tenderness, but no red flags. We want to avoid over-reliance on IV narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to try a right upper quadrant ultrasound to check your gallbladder and liver. It might help explain the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want it. It won’t show anything new. I’ve had so many. Just give me my meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But imaging could rule out other issues. We’ll respect your choice, but we still need to manage this safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your G-tube site has a small area of redness—about 3 cm—but no pus. We’ll keep an eye on it. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been like that for a while. Doesn’t hurt much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a MRSA screen from your nose today. It came back negative, so no need for isolation or special antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s MRSA again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a type of bacteria that can be resistant to antibiotics. You don’t have it, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been here a few days. Your breathing is fine, pain is stable, and nausea is improving. We’d like to try clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure I can keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start small—water, broth. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance to soft foods. Your insulin will need adjusting as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you kept the clear liquids down. We’re upgrading you to a soft diet for dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I still feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But you’re not vomiting, and you’re not in distress. That’s progress. We’ll keep anti-nausea meds available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You ate most of your meals yesterday—chicken, rice, even ice cream. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still achy. I need my Dilaudid. Can I get the IV kind again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re eating well and look comfortable. Given that, we’re switching to oral pain meds only—your regular 2 mg tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But that’s not enough. I need more. I’ve been in pain for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand your history of chronic pain. But we also need to balance safety and long-term management. Your primary doctor limits your Dilaudid for a reason.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A team meeting was held today—doctors, nurses, addiction specialist. We’re concerned about frequent hospital visits for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not making it up. The pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not saying it’s not. But we need a plan that supports you without increasing dependency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been off IV meds, eating regular food, and your blood sugar is stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge? But I still need pain meds. I need IV Dilaudid for my birthday next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I checked with your pharmacy. Your doctor prescribes 2 mg tablets on a set schedule. No IV refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But someone took my pills. I need a new prescription.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I can give you a prescription for 30 tablets of 2 mg, no refills. You’ll need to see your doctor for more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not enough. If you don’t give me more, I’ll just come back to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re frustrated. But we have to follow safe prescribing. Your primary team is your best resource for ongoing pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged home. You’re alert, walking, eating, and your diabetes is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still hurt. Why are you sending me out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you’re medically stable. We’re sending you home with your regular meds, including Dilaudid as prescribed. Please follow up with your doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But this isn’t over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We care about your well-being. Take care, and please reach out to your team if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and prescriptions now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to call your doctor for follow-up, especially about your pain and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And monitor your G-tube site. If it gets red, swollen, or painful, let someone know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You were brought in from another hospital because your blood sugar was very high and you're having abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I ran out of my fast-acting insulin—Novolog—two days ago. I couldn’t refill it yet. Then I started feeling really sick, and the pain in my belly came on strong overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were in DKA—diabetic ketoacidosis—but your numbers are improving. Your anion gap has mostly closed. We’re giving you fluids and starting your long-acting insulin, Lantus, while we confirm your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But the pain is bad. It’s in the middle, then moves to my right side. It’s sharp. Worse with food and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your abdomen. It shows new swelling and fluid around your pancreas. This means you’re having an episode of acute pancreatitis on top of your chronic condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like before? But I didn’t drink alcohol this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it can flare without alcohol. Not taking insulin properly can also contribute. We’ll keep you NPO—for now—so your pancreas can rest. You’ll get nutrition through your IV and your meds through your GJ tube if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being NPO. Can’t I just have a little?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Eating too soon can make the pain worse and delay healing. We’ll start with clear liquids once your pain improves and we see your labs trending down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I need pain medicine. I can’t stand this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV Dilaudid for pain. We’ll adjust the dose to keep you comfortable. It’s important you don’t refuse your insulin, though. Your blood sugar is still high, and we need to control it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want it. I think the dose is too high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can discuss the dose. But you do need insulin. If you continue to refuse, we may need to involve security to ensure your safety. This is for your own protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not fair!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re in pain and frustrated. We’re here to help. Let’s work together. Can we agree on a dose that feels safe to you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe 4 units less on the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try that. We’ll monitor your glucose closely. Your lipase was 295 on admission—elevated—and it jumped to 1,866 this morning. That’s your highest ever. So we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wow. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the inflammation is significant. But no complications like pseudocysts or blood clots were seen on the CT. That’s good. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your nausea has improved. You’re still NPO, but we’re giving Zofran for nausea as needed. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. Can I try some ice chips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can have ice chips. We’ll start slow. If you do well, we can try clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase is starting to come down. That’s a good sign. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today—broth, apple juice. But if you eat solids too soon, we’ll have to stop again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have crackers? Just a few?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. That could flare your pain. Let’s stick to liquids for now. Your body needs time to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so angry! I need more pain medicine now!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re in pain. But we’re already giving the maximum safe dose. Increasing it further isn’t safe. Let’s try calming techniques or your diazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No! I want more Dilaudid!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t do that. If you become aggressive, we’ll need to call security for everyone’s safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then get out!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Security is on the way. You’ll have a 24-hour detail after this. We’ll talk again when you’re calmer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you broke your GJ tube last night during an outburst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was upset. I didn’t mean to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been replaced today. But I need to be clear: if you break it again, it won’t be replaced. Nutrition says you can eat enough by mouth. It’s not medically necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I use it for meds when I’m NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. But going forward, if you damage it, it stays out. Please think carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Your lipase is down, and your pain is improving. We’re going to try full liquids today—pudding, yogurt. How are you sleeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. Can I have my nighttime meds? Benadryl, Ambien, the others?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your full regimen: Benadryl, Trazodone, Remeron, Ambien. But we’re keeping Benadryl at 100mg—no more—because higher doses caused urinary retention before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. You tolerated full liquids. We’re advancing to soft solids today—mashed potatoes, scrambled eggs. But no rushing to sandwiches or ice cream. That set you back before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting enteral nutrition through your GJ tube today, just to supplement, not replace eating. It’s 10 cc/hr, only if you want it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why? I’m eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a backup. You’re doing well, but we want to make sure you’re getting enough calories during recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Glucose is stable, lipase is down. You’re walking more, and your abdomen is soft and not tender. We’re very close to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been so anxious this whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve involved psychiatry. They recommend starting Celexa 10mg daily to help with anxiety and mood. Would you be open to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I think I need something more than just Valium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll start it today. Also, your insulin dose has been adjusted. You’re now on 40 units Lantus at night—lower than before—to prevent lows as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had three days of solid food without pain flares. That’s excellent. We’re planning discharge in a few days if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oral Dilaudid—2mg every 3 hours as needed. But please use it sparingly. We want to avoid frequent ER visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve created a new care plan with your input and your PCP’s. It will guide future admissions—things like pain med limits, insulin agreements, and no GJ tube replacement if broken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try to follow it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final labs look good. Glucose 332, but stable. No acidosis. Abdomen soft. You’re medically ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your insulin as prescribed—don’t skip Novolog. Eat small, frequent meals. Use pain meds only as needed. Take Celexa daily. And follow up with your PCP and endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll have a limited supply of Dilaudid and a 30-day prescription for Celexa with two refills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m sorry for how I acted sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re human. We’re here to help, not judge. The important thing is you’re going home healthier. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your insulin, eat regularly, take Celexa, and call your doctor if pain returns. We’ll see you soon for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve made great progress. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in tonight. You were having very high blood sugar, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was over 600 earlier. I took my Lantus and Humalog, but it’s not coming down like it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned fevers up to 104 and mouth ulcers this week. Are those still bothering you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The fever broke yesterday, but my mouth still hurts. I can’t eat much. I’m on acyclovir for the sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The high sugars and ketones in your urine mean you’re in a state called diabetic ketoacidosis, even though your blood work doesn’t show an acid buildup. We’ll keep an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I feel okay now. Why did I need to come back so soon after my last hospital stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even if you feel stable, very high sugars with ketones can be dangerous. We want to get your levels under control safely before sending you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach pain is back too—same as always, in the middle, going to my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your exam shows epigastric tenderness. But your lipase is normal, so it’s likely your chronic pain from gastroparesis or pancreatitis, not a new flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in two days. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gastroparesis and pain meds can slow things down. We’ll monitor that. For now, we’re continuing your home insulin—90 units Lantus and sliding scale Humalog.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is improving—it’s in the 200s now. We ran tests for flu and a urine culture. Both came back negative, so no infection we can find.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the fevers were just from the virus? Not something serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks that way. No sign of bacterial infection, white count is normal, and you’re not spiking fevers now. We think it was a viral illness that triggered the high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat something? I’m really hungry, but I’m scared it’ll make my stomach hurt worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to oral Dilaudid and you’ve tolerated sips. You can try a light breakfast. Start small and let us know how you feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well today—eating, pain controlled, sugars stable. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get a new prescription for pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Per your narcotics agreement, your primary care provider will manage all pain prescriptions, even after discharge. We won’t be writing any here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. And my insulin? Should I keep doing the same thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your 90 units Lantus at night and Humalog as needed. Watch for high sugars, especially if you’re sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my mouth sores? They make it hard to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking acyclovir as prescribed. Stick to soft, bland foods and stay hydrated. If they don’t improve, follow up with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach pain—should I go to the ER every time it flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. If your lipase stays normal and you’re not vomiting or spiking fevers, it’s likely your chronic condition. But always check your sugars and ketones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. A nurse will go over instructions and your follow-up plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel better knowing it’s not something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling really off—tired, achy, and my stomach hurts more than usual. It’s on the right side now, not the left like normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a few days. I also had a cough and burning when I pee. My doctor gave me Cipro for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about your blood sugar? I see it was very high in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was over 600. I used 30 units of Humalog and it didn’t budge. I turned my insulin pump off yesterday when I changed the site… I forgot to turn it back on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain the high sugar. We gave you insulin and fluids through an IV. Your levels are coming down now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also felt burning and swelling after taking my meds—Cipro, Neurontin, and cough syrup. I went to urgent care and got Benadryl.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a possible reaction. We’ve stopped the Cipro for now. The urine culture showed contamination, so no active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried it was a bad infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not seeing signs of that. Your lungs are clear, and the cough is likely from congestion. No fever now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my stomach pain? It’s different this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound. It was hard to get good images because of positioning, but we didn’t see gallstones or blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were a bit high, but they’re improving. It could be related to your chronic pancreatitis. The pain pattern has changed, so we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had pancreatitis before. My doctors wanted to do an MRCP with secretin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we tried to schedule that while you were here, but anesthesia wasn’t available. You mentioned you’d prefer to do it outpatient?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want to stay longer than I have to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Your PCP and gastroenterologist will coordinate it. For now, we’re managing your pain with Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning show your glucose is 252—much better. Sodium is normalizing too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting you on a regular diabetic diet. We’ve increased your Lantus insulin to 30 units at night as your intake improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually use my insulin pump between meals. Should I start that again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endocrinologist recommends stopping the pump. It’s not part of your official regimen and may have contributed to the high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it helps me control spikes after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but without proper oversight, it can be risky. We’ll stick to your prescribed sliding scale with Humalog for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are trending down—ALT and AST are lower. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fatty liver from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The ultrasound showed echogenic liver, which often means fatty infiltration. We can’t rule out fibrosis, but it’s not acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having chest tightness. Is that from the asthma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed sinus tachycardia, but no new changes. The tightness was pleuritic—likely from coughing. It’s improved, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little. I’m still using my inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using them as prescribed. We’ll continue monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your glucose is stable, and your pain is better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? What about the lung nodules from my old CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re likely inflammatory, but we recommend a follow-up chest CT in three months to check them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’m on a contract with my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your usual Dilaudid prescription. No new narcotics were given here, per your agreement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your primary doctor. She’ll help schedule the MRCP and review your insulin plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re doing much better—glucose under control, pain improved, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot clearer than when I came in. Thanks for helping me get back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call your doctor if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having really bad stomach pain again. It’s been worse lately, and last night I had a fever up to 103 and some bloody diarrhea.

conversation_lines.text: I’m scared it’s going to flare up again. I can’t keep living like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re monitoring you closely. For now, we’re keeping you NPO — nothing by mouth — just to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m so hungry. Can I have just a cracker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s wait a few hours. We’ll check your labs and see how you’re doing. We don’t want to trigger another attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Can I eat something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can try clear liquids. If you tolerate that, we can move to soft foods tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain? Still bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there. I took my Dilaudid, but it’s not helping as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you IV fluids and pain meds. Since you’re not vomiting and labs are okay, we’ll switch you to oral pain medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to go home. I’m tired of being here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard, but we want to make sure you’re safe. You were very anxious after the procedure, and we need to monitor you a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You slept okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I kept waking up. I took my usual sleep meds — trazodone, Benadryl, Ambien.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep those going. Your blood sugar was a bit high overnight, but we adjusted your insulin. You’re on Lantus at night and Humalog as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate this diabetes. It makes everything worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But you’re managing it as best you can. We’ll make sure your insulin plan stays consistent at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a chest X-ray yesterday — showed mild atelectasis, probably from shallow breathing due to pain. No pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not serious. Just means your lungs aren’t fully expanding. Deep breathing and walking will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been sipping broth and eating crackers — any nausea or pain after eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, actually I feel better. The pain is still there but not worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. It means your pancreas is tolerating food. We’ll keep you on oral pain meds and plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as you’re stable. But you’ll need to come back in two weeks to have the stent removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my anxiety? It gets so bad sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your Valium as needed. Please keep in touch with your mental health provider. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, walking, eating, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your insulin as prescribed. Use your pain meds as needed, but stick to your agreement with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up in two weeks for stent removal. If you develop fever, severe pain, or vomiting, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my cough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your inhalers. If the cough worsens or you run a fever, call your PCP. And please take those antibiotics you were prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to help. Take care, and see you soon for your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge meds and instructions. You’re doing well — just keep in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with abdominal pain and nausea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s my usual pain—epigastric and right upper quadrant, radiating to my back. It’s been worse the last two days. I haven’t eaten anything in a few days because I feel so nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The EGD went well. We successfully removed the pancreatic stent. It was still in place at the major papilla, and there were no complications.

conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I’ll feel better soon?

conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s changed? I’ll still have pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated dinner well, which is great. Your blood sugar is more stable, and you’re not showing signs of infection. We’re planning to discharge you soon.

conversation_lines.text: Okay. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your medications as prescribed. For insulin, start with 20 units of Lantus at bedtime. If your appetite improves, you may need to increase it—possibly up to 40 units. Use your Humalog as directed by your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain flares up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can take hydromorphone every three hours as needed, or ibuprofen every six hours. If nausea returns, use the prochlorperazine. And call your doctor if things worsen or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I follow up with anyone?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, stay in touch with your primary care provider and endocrinology team. They can help adjust your insulin. And keep managing your asthma with Advair and albuterol as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—your mental status is clear, you’re alert, and you’re walking fine. We’re clearing you to go home.
