conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired and anxious. I couldn’t sleep last night. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Benadryl and Dilaudid earlier. Ativan didn’t help, you said. We can restart your usual diazepam if you’d like—it’s on your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. The Benadryl helps me relax a bit, but I need the diazepam. And can I get Dilaudid again? The pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you Dilaudid as scheduled. We’re monitoring your pain and will keep using your regular home plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your anion gap has normalized, and your glucose is down to 180. That means the DKA is resolving. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my stomach still hurts, especially on the right side. Is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lipase—it’s normal. The ultrasound didn’t show gallstones or liver issues. Given your history, we think it’s likely related to your chronic pancreatitis, not an acute flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no change in my pain meds? I’m worried I won’t get enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home regimen—Dilaudid, gabapentin, and ibuprofen as needed. We’ll advance your diet today since your DKA is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HbA1c came back at 9.3%. That confirms your sugars have been high over the last few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I struggle with it. But I take my glargine every night. Is that still the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re keeping you on your usual insulin—70 units at bedtime and the sliding scale. No changes, to avoid confusion when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit shaky. Is my potassium okay? I remember last time it dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good catch. Your potassium was low this morning—3.0. We’re giving it through your IV to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take it by mouth instead? I don’t like NG tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You refused the NG tube, which is fine. We’re doing IV repletion only. We won’t force any tests or treatments you’re not comfortable with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes were slightly high on admission, but that was likely from a hemolyzed blood sample. A repeat test was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my liver? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of liver disease. The ultrasound was clear, and your bile ducts are normal. Nothing concerning there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your glucose is stable, and you’ve been eating without nausea. We’re switching you back to oral meds completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not quite yet. We want to make sure your potassium stays up and you remain stable on your own insulin. Probably one more night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got upset yesterday when I couldn’t get my Dilaudid on time. I didn’t mean to yell. I just get anxious when my pain’s not controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We reviewed it—the team knows your needs. We also clarified your meds. Turns out you weren’t actually taking Actos, so we removed it from your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t even realize it was still listed. That could’ve caused problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your potassium is still 3.0. We’ll keep giving IV potassium and monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another blood draw. Can we skip the next check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You refused the repeat potassium check, and that’s noted. We’ll continue treatment but respect your decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. You’ve been stable overnight. Your glucose is 123, and you’re alert and eating well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Are my meds the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no changes. You’ll go home on your usual insulin, pain meds, and other prescriptions. We added Prochlorperazine for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I should follow up with my primary doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Please see your PCP soon to review everything. You’re doing much better. We’ll get the discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the hospital because your blood sugar was very high and you were in diabetic ketoacidosis. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in a lot of pain. My stomach hurts like before, and I’ve been nauseous. I need my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve started you on IV fluids and insulin to treat the ketoacidosis. Your glucose was 595 when you arrived. We’re giving you pain medication through your IV for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take my insulin at home. I don’t know why this happened again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look into that. Your lipase was normal, so it doesn’t look like acute pancreatitis. But we know you have chronic pancreatitis, so we’ll manage your pain carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have chest pain. Is something wrong with my port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows the port is in place and there’s no pneumonia. We’ll keep an eye on it. The chest pain might be related to the port site or muscle strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your anion gap is starting to close, which means the DKA is improving. We’ll transition you to subcutaneous insulin soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat? I’m really hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once your labs stabilize, you can start with clear liquids. We’ll monitor your blood sugar closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your blood culture results back. You have Klebsiella in your blood, which explains the fever and high heart rate yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Did it come from my port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely. The bacteria are sensitive to ciprofloxacin, so we’re starting IV antibiotics. We’ll also check the port site for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The swab from your port site grew coagulase-negative staph. It’s not a full-blown abscess, but it’s infected. We need to remove the port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I don’t want it removed. I need it for my treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but with an active infection, leaving it in could make you sicker. We’ll place a PICC line in your right arm so we can continue antibiotics safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine, but I don’t want anyone forcing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed no clot in your arm, and no abscess near the port. That’s good. We’re scheduling the port removal and PICC placement for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under general anesthesia, so you won’t feel anything. You’ll wake up with a new line in your right arm and the old port gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. Your port was removed, and the PICC is in place. The tissue from the port pocket also grew coagulase-negative staph, so we’re continuing vancomycin for 19 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel sore. Can I have my Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on your regular 6 mg every 3 hours as needed. We’ll keep monitoring your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I need to talk about your insulin. Your doses have been increasing because your blood sugars are still high, even in the 400s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m taking it like I’m supposed to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed you’ve been injecting into your deltoid. That can affect absorption. We recommend injecting into your abdomen. Also, we’re increasing your long-acting insulin and adding NPH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I fell yesterday when I was walking around. I hit my head on the desk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw the note. The head CT was normal—no bleeding or fracture. You didn’t lose consciousness, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel fine now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. But please call for help if you’re unsteady. We don’t want another fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest chest X-ray shows the PICC tip is in the lower SVC. Your lungs still show low volumes, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My chest still hurts where the port was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: An ultrasound showed a small 3 cm fluid collection, likely a hematoma from the surgery. It should resolve on its own. We’ll keep the area clean and monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures since starting antibiotics have been negative. That’s great—no more bacteria in your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The infection is responding. Your abdominal pain is also better, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I pulled out my G-tube. I don’t need it if I can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it with your PCP. Since you’re tolerating food, we won’t reinsert it. But you’ll need to keep up with nutrition at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count is down to normal. That’s another sign the infection is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. You’ll finish your IV antibiotics, and we’ll remove the PICC before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your insulin. Because you need such high doses, you’ll be on U500 regular insulin—70 units at each meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s stronger than what I was on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s more concentrated. You’ll need fewer injections but the same total insulin. Your PCP will help you adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been low at times. It’s likely from the Dilaudid and dehydration. We’re encouraging fluids and watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t feel dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll keep monitoring. It improves with fluids, so stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed 10 days of vancomycin and ciprofloxacin. Your last blood cultures are negative. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I stop the IV now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. You need 19 days total. We’ll remove the PICC the day before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CBC and electrolytes are normal. The infection is resolved. We’ll remove the PICC tomorrow, and you can go home the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s your choice. If you need frequent IV access in the future, it can be discussed then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to manage my pain and insulin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your Dilaudid as prescribed and the new insulin regimen. Follow up with your PCP within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your PICC is out, and you’re cleared to go home. We’ve given you all your prescriptions and supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: take your insulin exactly as prescribed, watch for signs of infection, and call your doctor if your pain or blood sugar gets out of control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to come back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best to help you stay healthy at home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my chest still feels tender. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the hematoma will take a few weeks to heal. Use pain meds as needed and keep the area clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin—what if my sugars go high again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar regularly. The U500 is strong, so follow the dosing exactly. Your PCP will help adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve made great progress. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting home. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. You’ve worked hard. Let’s get your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last question—should I worry about the Klebsiella coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you keep your lines clean and follow your insulin plan, the risk is low. We treated it fully, so it should be gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can to prevent that. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Keep building on this progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now go home and rest. You’ve earned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having fevers at home, up to 102.7, and pain where my port was taken out. It’s been bothering me for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any other symptoms—like chills, cough, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, a little shortness of breath when I walk, and a dry cough. Also some nausea, but no vomiting lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your blood sugar—how has that been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High. I’ve been struggling to get my U500 insulin. Pharmacy delays again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure we confirm your dose with pharmacy. We checked your glucose in the ER—it was 333. No anion gap, so not DKA this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another DKA scare. But I refused insulin in the ER until I got pain meds. I was in a lot of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You got 6 mg of Dilaudid, and we gave a small dose of insulin. We’ll keep managing your pain and sugars together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What about the fever? Is it infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking. You had a chest ultrasound before coming in—showed a 2.4 cm area of phlegmon, but no abscess. No drainage or redness on exam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Phlegmon? Is that an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means inflammation in the tissue, possibly from your recent port removal. But no pus, so no need for drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the fever at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We drew blood cultures and labs. Your white count was a bit high in the ER, but now it’s coming down. Cultures are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Clear. No pneumonia or fluid. ECG showed sinus tachycardia, which makes sense with fever and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had a headache. Frontal. But no neck stiffness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—no nuchal rigidity. Likely tension or from the fever. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative after 24 hours. No bacteria growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in the blood. Your white count is now normal. The fever hasn’t returned since you’ve been here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the phlegmon? Shouldn’t I be on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given no fever, normal WBC, and no signs of active infection, we don’t think antibiotics are needed. The inflammation may be from healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my CRP and ESR are high—CRP 7.0 and ESR 91?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are elevated, but they can stay high for weeks after an infection or surgery. Likely reflecting ongoing healing from your port removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just wait it out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll monitor, but no further imaging or treatment is needed now. We’ll follow up with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back—showed mixed flora, likely contamination. No UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diabetes? I’m still worried about my insulin access.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We confirmed your U500 dose with pharmacy—70 units with each meal. You can continue your sliding scale as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll call them today. Any changes to my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. You’re on your usual pain meds, asthma inhalers, omeprazole, and mirtazapine. We’ll keep all the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update—your blood cultures remained negative. You’ve been afebrile all night, eating well, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you today. No antibiotics, no new treatments. Just follow up with your doctor as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-J tube? I’m supposed to get it replaced soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as scheduled. You’re tolerating food now, but the plan stands. Keep in touch with that team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain at the port site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your usual pain meds. The tenderness should improve. If it gets red, warm, or you spike a fever, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the ICU now. We're taking care of you for diabetic ketoacidosis. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really sick. Nauseous, throwing up, and this awful pain in my upper belly. It’s like my pancreas is on fire.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your labs show you were in DKA—diabetic ketoacidosis. That means your blood sugar was very high and your body was making ketones. We’ve started fluids and insulin to fix that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I missed some insulin. I just couldn’t keep up. But the pain—it’s not always from DKA, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're right. Your pain is likely related to your chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic issues. But right now, the DKA is the main problem. We’ll manage your pain too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. Eight weeks ago. It keeps coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we see your history. You have pancreatic divisum and scarring, which makes you prone to this. But today, the DKA is what brought you in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re responding well. Your blood sugar is coming down, and you’re getting better. We’ll keep you in the ICU tonight, then move you to the regular floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs improved overnight. Blood sugar is 292, anion gap is closing. We’re stopping the insulin drip soon and switching to shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shots? I was on U500 at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re switching to U100 Regular insulin because it’s easier to get at pharmacies. You know how to use both, so we’ll go with what’s available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that’s fine. But I need my pain meds. I’m hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your Dilaudid 6mg every 3 hours as needed. You can take it now if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. The pain is bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re transferring you to the medicine floor this afternoon. Your vitals are stable, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But where will I go after? I don’t have a place right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on that. Social work found temporary housing for you. You’ll have a place to go when you’re discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been so stressed about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your blood sugar is 180 this morning—much better. We’re keeping you on the new insulin schedule. Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but not like before. The prochlorperazine helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep it as needed. Your lipase was normal, so no sign of acute pancreatitis this time—just the chronic pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain isn’t from a flare-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. It’s likely from your chronic condition and the DKA. As your body recovers, the pain should ease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1c came back—it’s 11.6%. That means your diabetes has been poorly controlled over the last few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I try, but sometimes I just can’t do it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not judging. We want to help. Diabetes education will talk to you today about ways to make it easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll listen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Blood sugar is steady, and you’ve had no vomiting. We’re planning to discharge you in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But what about my meds? I lost everything when I left my last place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a 7-day supply of all your medications when you leave. That’ll give you time to get them refilled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And the insulin? Will I go back to U500?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use U100 for now. If you need U500 later, your doctor can help, but U100 is what’s available in most pharmacies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are normal now. Blood sugar is 130, no ketones. You’re almost ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I’m scared I’ll end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. That’s why we’re stressing follow-up. You’ll see your PCP soon, and we’ll help connect you with support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a guardian. She helps me make decisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve spoken with her. She supports your care plan, so we can move forward safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ve done really well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. No pain, not nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll send you home with your meds, instructions, and follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see a specialist for my pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re scheduled to follow up with gastroenterology. They’ll manage your chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health? I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your behavioral health provider. We know this is hard, and support is available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’re alert, pain-free, and labs are stable. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—take your insulin, manage your diet, and call if you’re not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do everything we can to help you stay healthy. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll get a ride to your new housing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve got it covered. And remember—your PCP appointment is in three days. Please go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine test showed benzodiazepines, but no other drugs. Just want to make sure you’re safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take diazepam for anxiety. It’s prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s on your list. Just confirming. All good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you soon. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Just ready to rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport is here. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You're in the hospital because of abdominal pain and high blood sugar. Can I ask what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It hurts so much. I haven’t eaten in six days. Every time I try, it makes me sick and my stomach burns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re in so much pain. We saw you had blood sugar of 490 when you came in, and your labs show mild diabetic ketoacidosis. That can make nausea and pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know my sugars have been high. I stopped my insulin a few days ago because I felt dizzy and weak, and I was scared of going low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense, but stopping insulin even when you're not eating can lead to DKA. We gave you some insulin in the ER and started fluids. Your acid levels are already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want pain medicine. Can I get something stronger? I need IV meds like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you're hurting, but your pain contract with your doctor says we can only give your usual oral Dilaudid. We can’t give IV narcotics. We also need to check your bag for extra medications for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No! I don’t want that. I want to go to another hospital. This isn’t fair!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear how upset you are. We’re here to help you safely. Let’s focus on getting your pain under control with your regular meds and treating your diabetes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I know yesterday was rough. We’d like to check your vitals and do some blood work to see how you’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want labs. I don’t want to be poked. The pain is still here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we need to monitor your blood sugar and electrolytes, especially with DKA. We’ll make it quick. Your Dilaudid is due—would you like that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. Just give me the pill. But I still want stronger medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your acid level improved from 23 to 16. That’s good progress. Your blood sugar is still high, around 330, but coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I still feel awful? I’m dizzy and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The dizziness could be from dehydration or the anti-nausea meds. We’re giving you fluids and added ondansetron and metoclopramide to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s still burning in my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on IV pantoprazole twice a day for possible gastritis. Your ultrasound showed no gallbladder issues—you’ve had that removed—and your liver looks normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I have pain in the upper right side too. Could it be my pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking about that. Your pancreas wasn’t well seen on ultrasound due to gas, but your history of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic divisum makes it a possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back with mixed bacteria, but it looks like contamination. No infection found. Blood cultures have no growth so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Symptoms lasting a week aren’t typical for viral gastroenteritis. We think it’s related to your diabetes and chronic abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with the diabetes team. There’s some confusion about your insulin. You’ve been taking U500, but it seems you were dosing it as if it were regular insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take 35 units in the morning. That’s what I always do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: U500 is five times stronger than regular insulin. So 35 units of U500 equals 175 units of regular insulin. But you’ve actually been getting only 35 regular insulin equivalents, which is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, so I’ve been under-dosing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. But because you weren’t eating, your needs were lower. The team adjusted your dose to 35 units breakfast, 25 lunch, 20 dinner of U500—still less than before—but safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not taking my old dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re keeping it lower because you’re eating less. Once you’re back to normal meals, your doctor will adjust it. For now, this helps avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your acid gap is normal. Electrolytes are stable. You’re doing well with the insulin adjustment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took a few sips of broth yesterday. Didn’t make the pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’d like you to try a soft diet today—maybe applesauce or crackers. If that goes well, you can move to regular food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain medicine? Can I take it with food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take your Dilaudid with food. We’re still not giving IV pain meds, but we’ll keep supporting you with your oral plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well today—ate a full lunch without pain worsening. That’s a big step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have a dull ache in my right side, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with ultrasound. No issues with your liver or bile ducts. The pain might be part of your chronic condition. We’ll keep managing it with your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed the ultrasound again. Liver and biliary tree are normal. Pancreas wasn’t visible, but no signs of acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing shows what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not definitively. It’s likely a flare of your chronic pancreatitis or gastritis. Since you’re eating and pain is improving, we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a full breakfast and lunch yesterday with no problems. Blood sugar is around 250—still high but stable. Dizziness is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t felt dizzy since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That was likely from the anti-nausea meds or dehydration. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re eating well, pain is controlled, and your diabetes is stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my insulin? I’m still confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on 35 units U500 at breakfast, 25 at lunch, 20 at dinner. This is less than before, but safer now. Don’t go back to your old dose until you see your diabetes doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my sugars go high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your sliding scale as directed. Call your doctor if sugar is over 400 or under 70. You have follow-up with your PCP tomorrow and diabetes specialist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I think I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain medicine stays the same—6 mg Dilaudid every 3 hours as needed. Keep taking your other home meds like mirtazapine and diazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No IV meds at home, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Your contract is for oral meds only. If pain worsens, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. A nurse will go over your discharge papers and meds before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little sore, but I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable—blood pressure 100/60, heart rate 80, oxygen 99%. You’re alert and walking fine. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in with a fever and some pain around your central line, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve had a fever since they put in that line. It wasn’t supposed to look like this—it was supposed to be a port, but now there’s a tube sticking out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like a Hickman line instead of a port. We’ll check the placement, but the chest X-ray shows it’s in the right spot in your vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I’ve been so tired and achy. Last night I spiked a fever to 103.9. I couldn’t sleep at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’ve been feeling so bad. We’re checking for infections—blood work, urine, and cultures. So far, nothing shows a clear source yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my neck hurts where the line goes in. Is it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s tenderness, but no redness or pus, which is reassuring. We’re watching it closely. We also heard some wheezing—do you have asthma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. It’s been worse the last couple of days. I’ve been coughing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray is clear, no pneumonia. But your lungs are tight. We’re going to start you on nebulizers to help with the wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I take something for pain? I just want to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we can give you your usual hydrocodone for pain. But we’ll monitor your breathing since you’re wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my blood sugar—I’ve been trying to keep it stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 108 when you came in—normal. But we know illness can make it rise. We’ll check it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, but still achy. How are the test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are still pending. Urine culture grew some bacteria, but it looks like contamination—probably from vaginal flora.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from the urine. We’re still waiting on blood. But your symptoms—fever, cough, wheezing—suggest a viral bronchitis, possibly triggering your asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been coughing so hard I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense with the coughing. Your abdomen is soft and not tender, so it’s not your chronic pain flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing the nebulizers. And we’d like to start a short course of oral steroids—prednisone—to calm your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? Won’t that mess up my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. That’s why we want to monitor you here. If your sugars go up, we can adjust your insulin. It’s safer than letting the asthma worsen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that makes sense. But I don’t want to go into DKA again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t let that happen. We’ll check your sugars every few hours and adjust your U500 insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your blood sugar went up to 420 last night after the first steroid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no! Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s high, but you didn’t develop ketones. We increased your U500 insulin under guidance from endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the new dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: 70 units at breakfast, 70 at lunch, and 50 at dinner. We’ll keep checking your sugars to make sure they stay in the 100s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s way more than before. I was only taking 14 units each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because U500 is 5 times stronger than regular insulin. So 70 units of U500 equals about 350 units of regular insulin, which is appropriate with steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I see. I always get confused with the dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have clear instructions when you go home. Your sugars are already coming down—119 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Less wheezing. You’re responding well to the steroids and nebs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you one more day to make sure your sugars stay stable and you finish a few more doses of steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was thinking of leaving today. I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but with the steroids, your sugars could spike again. And if you go into DKA, it could be serious. Your guardian has been contacted for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be here, but I don’t want to get worse either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just one more night. We’ll keep you comfortable and make sure everything is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood sugars have been in the 100s all night. The endocrine team signed off on your discharge insulin plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever since yesterday. Blood cultures came back negative. We think it was a viral illness, not a line infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow morning. You’ll finish your prednisone at home—7 days total. Keep using your inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin? I’ll need help remembering the new dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a printed sheet. Breakfast and lunch: 70 units of U500. Dinner: 50. Check sugars four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your primary doctor in a week. And please call if you develop fever, trouble breathing, or high sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Breathing easier. No fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember—finish the prednisone, monitor sugars, and care for your line as instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—what about the sore throat and those little sores in my mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw the vesicles. They’re likely viral, part of the same illness. They should heal on their own in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I was worried it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. Just part of what you’ve been through. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. I’m going straight to bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Get some rest. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in follow-up.
